planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; an early Israeli-origin cultivar that reliably fruits within a couple of years of transplanting, making it a good pick for growers who want a quicker payoff than seedling-grown loquats.

directions: Emanuel is an Israeli-origin loquat cultivar valued for its early ripening season, with medium-sized fruit typically ready in February through March in warm climates like the Gulf Coast. The thin-skinned, dark yellow-to-orange fruit encloses juicy, mildly sweet flesh with two to three seeds. Like all loquats, Emanuel blooms in fall and winter, so a hard freeze during bloom or early fruit set can wipe out the crop for that year, making a sheltered planting site valuable in zone 9a. Grafted trees begin bearing within a couple of years of transplanting.

common_name: Ellen Marker Loquat (Modern Florida Seedling Selection with Creamy White Flesh)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, full-sun to partial-shade sites; a recently introduced Florida seedling selection, so let fruit color fully to yellow-orange before picking to develop its full flavor.

directions: Ellen Marker is a modern Florida seedling selection introduced in 2020 by fruit explorer Craig Hepworth, chosen for its large, pear-shaped fruit and complex flavor. The creamy white flesh combines classic loquat peach-apricot notes with a brighter, almost grape-like tartness when fruit is left to fully color to yellow-orange before picking. As with other loquats, its fall-to-winter bloom period leaves flowers and young fruit vulnerable to hard freezes, an important consideration for Gulf Coast growers when choosing a planting site. Being a relatively new selection, its performance and self-fruitfulness outside Florida are still being documented by home growers.

planting.note: Plant grafted, self-fertile trees in spring in full sun; also sold as Jehuda, a vigorous Israeli cultivar that reaches medium tree size and typically begins bearing three to five years after transplanting.

directions: Yehuda, also spelled Jehuda, is an Israeli loquat cultivar prized for large, light-orange, apricot-shaped fruit with a thick skin that peels away to reveal richly sweet flesh some growers describe as mango-like when fully ripe. It is self-fertile and typically begins bearing three to five years after transplanting, with flowers opening from December through February. Loquat blossoms and young fruit are cold-tender, so a hard freeze during this winter bloom window can reduce or eliminate the following spring's crop even though the tree itself tolerates considerable cold. Yehuda is a vigorous grower that reaches medium size at maturity.

common_name: Peluche Loquat (Large Sweet Spanish Commercial Loquat)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a Spanish commercial cultivar noted for unusually large, high-sugar fruit, one of the largest and sweetest loquat varieties grown.

directions: Peluche is a Spanish loquat cultivar grown commercially in the Mediterranean and recognized as one of the largest and sweetest loquat varieties available, with fruit weighing around 70 grams and notably high sugar content. Like other loquats, Peluche flowers in fall and winter, so its blossoms and developing fruit can be damaged by a hard freeze, a real risk during Gulf Coast cold snaps even in zone 9a. The deep orange skin and flesh are typical of the sweeter Mediterranean cultivars, and the fruit ripens mid-to-late season. Peluche is grown alongside cultivars like Algerie in Spain's loquat-producing regions.

common_name: Magdal Loquat (Major Spanish Commercial Sweet-Flavored Loquat)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; one of the handful of cultivars grown at commercial scale in Spain and is known for a sweeter flavor than tarter selections like Algerie.

directions: Magdal is one of only a handful of loquat cultivars grown commercially at scale in Spain, particularly in Andalusia, where it is valued alongside Golden Nugget for its notably sweet flavor. Fruit ripens with the orange skin and flesh typical of top commercial Mediterranean cultivars, and sensory panels have consistently rated Magdal among the sweeter-tasting loquats compared to tarter selections like Algerie. As with all loquats, Magdal blooms in autumn and winter, so a hard freeze during bloom or early fruit development can severely reduce or eliminate that year's harvest. Grafted trees typically need two to three years after transplanting before first fruiting.

common_name: Lovett Loquat (Early-Ripening Florida Seedling with Honey-Sweet White Flesh)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; a Florida seedling selection prized for early ripening and honey-sweet white flesh, well suited to Gulf South dooryard planting.

directions: Lovett is a Florida seedling selection known for honey-sweet, white-fleshed fruit of medium size, ripening in early spring ahead of many standard cultivars. Like other loquats, Lovett blooms in fall and early winter, leaving its flowers and small developing fruit exposed to occasional hard freezes that can reduce Gulf Coast harvests in a cold winter. The tree performs well in the humid Gulf South climate where it originated and is grown as a dooryard fruit tree valued for its mild, dessert-quality flavor. Loquats are generally self-fertile, though fruit set is often heaviest when more than one tree is nearby.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; a classic early-ripening Japanese cultivar that fruits quickly after transplanting and can even produce two crops a year in subtropical climates.

directions: Nagasakiwase is a classic Japanese loquat cultivar and one of the earliest-ripening varieties available, producing medium to large fruit with deep orange, exceptionally juicy flesh and a high flesh-to-seed ratio. The flavor combines apricot and pineapple notes with a mild tang, and in warm subtropical climates the tree can produce two crops per year. Because loquats bloom in fall and winter, Nagasakiwase's early habit means its flowers and young fruit are exposed to the coldest part of the Gulf Coast winter, so a late freeze can still damage the crop despite the tree's overall vigor. Grafted trees are fast to bear, often fruiting within two to three years of transplanting.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun with room to spread; flowers about a month later than most cultivars, extending the harvest season and giving its blossoms a slight edge over early winter cold snaps.

directions: Enormity is a large-fruited loquat selection with extra-large, oval, golden-yellow to orange fruit and juicy, sweet flesh carrying apricot and pineapple notes. It flowers about a month later than most standard cultivars, which extends the loquat harvest season and can offer some protection from the earliest winter freezes that damage the blossoms of earlier-flowering varieties. Even so, because loquats bloom in the cooler months, a hard freeze during Enormity's later fall-to-winter bloom period can still reduce fruit set. The tree is vigorous and needs a few years to reach bearing size after transplanting.

common_name: Bessell Brown Loquat (Compact Large-Fruited Loquat Grafted on Quince Rootstock)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun to partial shade; typically grafted onto quince rootstock, producing a compact tree well suited to smaller Gulf Coast landscapes while still yielding full-sized fruit.

directions: Bessell Brown is a large-fruited loquat cultivar typically grafted onto quince rootstock to produce a compact, small tree suited to smaller Gulf Coast gardens. The fruit has thick, bruise-resistant orange skin and firm, golden flesh with a mild flavor reminiscent of pear, apricot, and pineapple. Because it is grafted onto quince, the tree stays notably smaller than seedling loquats while still producing full-sized fruit, though the dwarfing rootstock does not change the plant's fundamental cold sensitivity during its fall-to-winter bloom period. A hard freeze while Bessell Brown is in flower or setting fruit can still reduce or eliminate that season's harvest.
